homily: Dear brothers and sisters, yesterday we celebrated the birth of Christ; today we celebrate the birth into heaven of the first martyr. But before Stephen was a martyr, he was a deacon who served at tables.

In the early Church in Jerusalem there was a complaint: the widows of the Greek-speaking Christians were being neglected in the daily distribution of food. The apostles asked the community to choose seven men of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to take care of this service. Stephen was the first named (Acts 6:1–6). His holiness began in a very practical task: making sure poor widows got their food.

Luke tells us that Stephen, full of grace and power, did great wonders and signs among the people, and that his opponents could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke (Acts 6:8–10). When he stood before the Council, his face was like the face of an angel (Acts 6:15). The man who served tables became a fearless witness. Faithfulness in small things prepared him for great things.

And when the stones began to fly, Stephen prayed with the words of his Master: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit; and kneeling down he cried out: Lord, do not hold this sin against them (Acts 7:59–60). He died as Jesus had died, entrusting himself to God and forgiving his killers. Among the witnesses was a young man named Saul, who would become the apostle Paul. Stephen's forgiveness bore fruit.

So Stephen gives us a Christmas programme: serve humbly, witness boldly, forgive completely. Is there someone in your family you have not forgiven? This is the season to let go. The Child in the manger came to make forgiveness possible. Let us ask St Stephen to help us live what we receive at this Holy Mass.

opts.a: Teaching homily: martyrdom and Christian witness
intro: Martyr means witness. Today let us understand why the Church honours martyrs so highly.

sub: A witness to the truth of faith, to the point of death (CCC 2473).
Bound to Christ by charity.
Not suicide, not violence; freely accepting death rather than denying Christ.
points.apply: Thank God for the martyrs of our own land.

points.h: The blood of martyrs is seed
sub: Tertullian's saying.
Persecution has never destroyed the Church.
Christians still die for their faith today.
points.apply: Pray for persecuted Christians today.

sub: Most of us are called to white martyrdom: daily fidelity.
Courage to speak and to act as Christians.
Gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15–16).
points.apply: Do not hide your faith at work or school this week.

concl: Martyrdom is the supreme witness, and every Christian is called to bear witness.
The Church today is still a Church of martyrs.
opts.resolve: This week I will pray for persecuted Christians and not hide my faith.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the word martyr comes from the Greek word for witness. The Catechism says that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: it means bearing witness even unto death; the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity (CCC 2473).

A martyr is not someone who seeks death or uses violence. The martyrs of the Church never killed anyone. They freely accepted death rather than deny Christ, and they died forgiving. Stephen is the first of a long line: the apostles, the martyrs of the Roman persecutions, the martyrs of Japan, Uganda, Vietnam, Mexico, and in our own land the martyr Devasahayam and many others.

In the second century Tertullian wrote that the blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians. After Stephen's death a severe persecution broke out and the believers were scattered, but those who were scattered went from place to place proclaiming the word (Acts 8:1–4). Persecution has never destroyed the Church; it has spread it. And today, more Christians suffer for their faith than at any time in history. Let us pray for them often.

Most of us will not be asked to shed our blood. But all of us are called to witness. The Fathers spoke of white martyrdom: the daily dying to self, fidelity in marriage and vocation, honesty when dishonesty would be easier, refusing to join in mockery of the faith. St Peter tells us always to be ready to give an account of the hope that is in us, yet with gentleness and reverence (1 Peter 3:15–16).

So on this second day of Christmas, let us thank God for the martyrs, pray for persecuted Christians, and ask for courage. The Child of Bethlehem was born to die for us; Stephen died for Him. At this Holy Mass let us ask for the grace to live for Him.
Dear brothers and sisters, Christmas is a feast of joy, yet today the Church remembers something terrible: the killing of the little children of Bethlehem.

King Herod heard from the wise men that a new king had been born. He was afraid of losing his power. He tried to trick the wise men and, when that failed, he sent soldiers to kill every boy of two years and under in Bethlehem.

But God protected his Son. An angel warned Joseph in a dream: get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt. And Joseph got up that very night and went. Silent, obedient Joseph saved the life of the Saviour.

Matthew recalls the prophet Jeremiah: a voice in Ramah, Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted. Scripture does not hide the grief of mothers. God sees every tear. And the Church honours these children as the first martyrs: they could not speak, but they confessed Christ by dying for him.

Today Herod has many faces. Children are still killed before birth, in wars, through hunger and abuse. The Holy Innocents ask us to stand with the weakest, to protect life from its beginning, and to comfort parents who grieve.
Jesus said: “Let the little children come to me, and do not stop them.” Let us bring all the children of the world to him today, and let us be like Joseph, ready to rise and act to protect them.
kids: Children, today we remember the baby boys of Bethlehem.
A bad king named Herod wanted to hurt baby Jesus. An angel told Joseph to take Jesus far away to Egypt, and Joseph obeyed.
The king hurt other babies, but Jesus took them to heaven. They are now saints!
Jesus loves every child. Let us pray today for children who are sick or in danger.

intro: The Holy Innocents died because a powerful man felt threatened by a child. Children are still in danger today.

sub: Power that feels threatened by a child.
Violence to protect position.
Herods in every age.
points.apply: Examine where fear makes you harsh.

sub: Grief of mothers (Jeremiah 31:15).
God hears the cry of the innocent.
Comfort for parents who have lost children.
points.apply: Pray for parents who have lost a child.

sub: The unborn, abused children, child labourers, refugee children.
Safe parishes and homes.
Every child is Christ's little one (Matthew 18:5–6).
points.apply: Support one concrete work for children in need.

concl: Christ identified Himself with the little ones; to protect them is to protect Him.
The feast calls us to be Josephs, not Herods.
opts.resolve: I will support one concrete work that protects children.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, three days after Christmas the Church remembers a terrible event. King Herod, afraid that the newborn King of the Jews would take his throne, ordered the killing of all the boys in and around Bethlehem who were two years old or under (Matthew 2:16). The Church honours these children as martyrs: they died in place of Christ.

Herod is a picture of power that feels threatened. He had palaces and soldiers, yet he was terrified of a baby. Fear makes people cruel. There are Herods in every age: those who sacrifice the weak to protect their comfort, position or wealth. And there is a little Herod in each of us when fear makes us harsh.

Matthew quotes the prophet: a voice was heard in Ramah, wailing and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be consoled, because they are no more (Matthew 2:18; Jeremiah 31:15). God hears that cry. Today let us pray for all parents who have lost a child, through illness, accident, violence or miscarriage. Their children are in God's hands.

And let us ask: where are the innocents in danger today? The unborn child whose life is not protected. Children who are abused, even, to our great shame, in some places within the Church. Children forced to work, children trafficked, children in refugee camps, children growing up without love. Jesus said that whoever welcomes a child in His name welcomes Him, and warned terribly against those who cause little ones to stumble (Matthew 18:5–6).

So this feast calls each of us to be a Joseph, not a Herod: to rise and protect the child. Make our homes and parishes safe places. Support works that care for children in need. Defend life from its beginning. At this Holy Mass let us offer all the innocent victims of our world to the Child of Bethlehem, who came to save them.

opts.a: Teaching homily: the dignity of the child and the right to life
intro: The Holy Innocents remind us of the Church's teaching on the dignity of every human life, especially the smallest.

sub: Human life is sacred from its beginning (CCC 2258).
The unborn child is a person from conception (CCC 2270).
No one may directly destroy an innocent human being.
points.apply: Pray for the protection of unborn children.

sub: Children are the supreme gift of marriage (CCC 2378).
Their education is a right and duty of parents.
Society must protect children (CCC 2211).
points.apply: Thank God for the children in your family.

sub: The Church's duty to protect minors.
Mercy and healing for those who have had or assisted an abortion.
Reconciliation through confession (CCC 2272).
points.apply: If you carry such a wound, come to confession: God's mercy is greater.

concl: The Church defends the child because Christ came as a child.
Truth about life and mercy toward sinners go together.
opts.resolve: I will pray daily for the protection of children and for mothers in difficulty.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the Holy Innocents were killed before they could speak a word, yet the Church has honoured them as martyrs since ancient times. Their feast invites us to recall the Church's teaching on the dignity of the child.

The Catechism teaches that human life is sacred because from its beginning it involves the creative action of God; God alone is the Lord of life from beginning to end; no one can claim the right directly to destroy an innocent human being (CCC 2258). Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception (CCC 2270). The prophet heard God say: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5). And the child John leaped in Elizabeth's womb at the presence of the unborn Christ (Luke 1:41).

Children are the supreme gift of marriage (CCC 2378). They are not property and not a burden, but persons entrusted to their parents. Parents have the first right and duty to educate them; society and the State have the duty to protect them (CCC 2211, 2221). Jesus took the children in His arms and blessed them, and said that the Kingdom belongs to such as these (Mark 10:14–16).

The Church also has a grave duty to protect minors in her own life. Every parish, school and institution must be a safe place. Where children have been harmed, the truth must be faced, victims must be heard and helped, and justice done.

At the same time, the Church proclaims mercy. If someone here carries the wound of abortion, in their own life or by assisting another, do not despair. The sin is grave, but God's mercy is greater. Come to confession; the Father runs to embrace the returning child (Luke 15:20). Let us offer this Holy Mass for all innocent victims, for mothers in difficulty, and for a culture that welcomes every child.

Dear friends, on this fifth day of the Christmas Octave St John writes: by this we may be sure that we know him, if we obey his commandments. Whoever says, I abide in him, ought to walk just as he walked (1 John 2:3, 6). Knowing Christ is not only an idea; it is a way of walking.

John continues: whoever says, I am in the light, while hating a brother or sister, is still in the darkness. Whoever loves a brother or sister lives in the light (1 John 2:9–10). Christmas light is tested by love.

In the Gospel Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the Temple. There the old man Simeon, righteous and devout, who had been waiting for the consolation of Israel, takes the child in his arms and praises God: Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation, a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:25–32).

Simeon waited his whole life, and his waiting was fulfilled in holding a baby. The Church prays his song every night at Compline, before sleep. It is the prayer of one who is at peace because he has seen Christ.

But Simeon also tells Mary: this child is destined for the falling and the rising of many, and a sword will pierce your own soul too (Luke 2:34–35). The light of Christmas already points to the Cross. Love costs.

Let us ask for Simeon's patience and peace. Let us walk as Jesus walked, loving our brothers and sisters, so that we truly live in the light. And tonight, before sleep, let us pray: now, Lord, let your servant go in peace. Amen.
kids: Children, old Simeon held baby Jesus and was so happy! We hold Jesus in our hearts when we receive Him with love.

homily: Dear friends, St John writes to Christians of every age: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven; to you, fathers, because you know him; to you, young people, because you have conquered the evil one (1 John 2:12–14). Every generation has its place in God's family.

Then he warns: do not love the world or the things in the world. The desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, the pride in riches, comes not from the Father. The world and its desire are passing away, but those who do the will of God live for ever (1 John 2:15–17).

In the Gospel we meet Anna, a prophet, eighty-four years old, a widow who never left the Temple but worshipped there with fasting and prayer night and day. At that moment she came, began to praise God and to speak about the child to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:36–38).
Anna was a widow for most of her life. She could have become bitter. Instead, she made her loneliness into prayer. And because she was praying, she was there at the right moment to meet the Messiah.
Then the Gospel says: the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom; and the favour of God was upon him (Luke 2:40). The Son of God grew up slowly, in an ordinary home in Nazareth.

At the end of this year, let us examine what we love: the passing things of the world, or the will of God that lasts for ever? Let us honour the widows and elderly in our parish, and learn from Anna to turn loneliness into prayer and praise. Amen.
kids: Children, Anna was very old and prayed every day. Thank God for your grandparents who pray for you!

homily: Dear friends, on the last day of the year St John writes: children, it is the last hour! Many antichrists have come (1 John 2:18). For Christians, every hour since Christ's coming is the last hour: a time of decision and of vigilance. But John reassures us: you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you know the truth (1 John 2:20).

The Gospel takes us back to the beginning: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things came into being through him. In him was life, and the life was the light of all people (John 1:1–4).
At the end of a year, we remember that time itself was made through the Word. Our years begin and end in him. He is the Alpha and the Omega.

John continues: the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory. From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace (John 1:14, 16). Grace upon grace: that is a good summary of the year that is ending. Even in difficulties, God's grace did not stop.

Tonight many will celebrate with fireworks and parties. That is fine. But let us also make time to thank God, to ask pardon for the sins of this year, and to entrust the new year to him. Many parishes hold a thanksgiving Mass or adoration at midnight.

Tomorrow the Church celebrates Mary, Mother of God, and prays for peace in the world. Let us begin the new year in the arms of the Mother and the Child. Grace upon grace: thank you, Lord, for this year. Amen.
kids: Children, tonight thank Jesus for all the good things this year. Ask Him to stay with you all next year!

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, on this first weekday of Advent Isaiah shows us a stump. The great family tree of David has been cut down; it looks dead. Yet the prophet says: a shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots (Isaiah 11:1). Advent begins with hope where everything seems finished.

Upon this shoot the Spirit of the Lord will rest: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might, of knowledge and the fear of the Lord (Isaiah 11:2). The Church sees here the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which Christ possesses in fullness and shares with us in Confirmation.

And the fruit of this King is peace: the wolf shall live with the lamb, the leopard lie down with the kid, and a little child shall lead them (Isaiah 11:6). It is a picture of creation healed. Old enemies are reconciled. The violence of the strong gives way to the trust of the small.

In the Gospel Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit and thanks the Father, because these things have been hidden from the wise and the intelligent and revealed to infants (Luke 10:21). God's secrets are opened not to the proud but to the little ones.

Advent asks us to become little again: to admit our need, to stop pretending to have everything under control, to receive like children. The little child of Isaiah's prophecy leads the wild animals; the little Child of Bethlehem will lead us to peace.

Is there a stump in your life, something that looks finished: a marriage, a vocation, a friendship, your prayer? Bring it to the Lord this Advent. He can make a shoot spring from it. And ask the Holy Spirit to renew his seven gifts in you, so that you may be ready for Christmas. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus was happy when little ones understood God. God loves to show His secrets to children. Thank Him today in a short prayer!

homily: Dear friends, Isaiah today describes a great banquet on the mountain of the Lord: a feast of rich food and well-aged wines for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6). It is a feast for all nations, not one people only. And at that feast God will destroy the shroud that covers all peoples; he will swallow up death forever and wipe away the tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:7–8).
This is the hope of Advent: not only a baby in a manger, but the final banquet of the Kingdom, where death is no more and every tear is wiped away. Christmas begins what that banquet will complete.

In the Gospel Jesus goes up a mountain by the Sea of Galilee. Great crowds come, bringing the lame, the blind, the mute and many others, and he heals them. Then he has compassion on the hungry crowd, and with seven loaves and a few fish he feeds four thousand. All ate and were filled, and seven baskets were left over (Matthew 15:29–37).

Notice the order: first Jesus heals, then he feeds. And notice his words: I have compassion for the crowd. Jesus sees physical hunger as well as spiritual hunger. Isaiah's mountain banquet is already beginning on the hillside in Galilee.

The disciples asked: where are we to get enough bread in the desert? They looked at what they lacked. Jesus asked: how many loaves have you? He looked at what they had. Advent invites us to give our little loaves to the Lord, our time, our money, our talents, and let him multiply them.

This Advent, let us feed someone who is hungry: a migrant worker, a poor family, a lonely person who needs company more than food. And at each Mass let us remember that we are already tasting the banquet of the Kingdom. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus fed thousands with just a few loaves. When you share even a little, Jesus can do great things with it!

homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate St Francis Xavier, patron of the missions, who preached along the coasts of South India in the sixteenth century. The Advent readings speak of building on solid ground.

Isaiah sings of a strong city with walls and ramparts: trust in the Lord for ever, for in the Lord God you have an everlasting rock (Isaiah 26:4). The proud city falls, but the poor and the needy walk securely on the rock.

Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with a parable. Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father. The one who hears my words and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on rock. The rain fell, the floods came, the winds blew, but the house did not fall (Matthew 7:21, 24–25).

Every Kerala family knows what floods can do. In 2018 we saw houses on weak foundations collapse, while others stood. Jesus says the difference is not in hearing but in doing. Many people hear the Gospel; fewer build their lives on it.

Francis Xavier built on the rock. He heard the words of Jesus, what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his soul, and he acted on them. He left a brilliant career in Paris, and spent himself for the poor fishermen of the Coromandel and Travancore coasts, teaching them the faith in their own language with songs and prayers.

This Advent, let us check our foundations. Is my faith only words, Lord, Lord, or is it action? Let us choose one word of Jesus and put it into practice this week. And let us pray for missionaries, that like St Francis Xavier they may build the Church on the rock of Christ. Amen.
kids: Children, a house on rock does not fall in a storm. When you obey Jesus, you are building on rock. St Francis Xavier did that!

homily: Dear friends, on this First Friday of December Isaiah promises a reversal: in a very little while Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field. On that day the deaf shall hear the words of a scroll, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see (Isaiah 29:17–18). The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord.

In the Gospel two blind men follow Jesus, crying out: have mercy on us, Son of David! It is a cry of faith; they call him by his messianic title. Jesus asks them: do you believe that I am able to do this? They say: yes, Lord. He touches their eyes and says: according to your faith let it be done to you (Matthew 9:27–29).
Jesus asks the same question of each of us this Advent: do you believe that I am able to do this? Able to heal your blindness, to change your heart, to restore your family, to forgive your sin?
There is a blindness worse than physical blindness: not seeing God's love, not seeing the needs of others, not seeing our own sins. The two blind men knew they were blind. Many of us do not.
On the First Friday we honour the Sacred Heart of Jesus. From that Heart flows the mercy the blind men begged for. The simplest prayer of the Church, Lord, have mercy, is their prayer.

Today, let us make their prayer ours. Let us name one blindness in our life and ask Jesus to touch it. If possible, let us go to confession and receive Holy Communion in honour of the Sacred Heart. And let us answer his question with faith: yes, Lord, I believe. Amen.
kids: Children, two blind men asked Jesus for help and He opened their eyes. When you pray, believe that Jesus can help you!

homily: Dear friends, Isaiah speaks tenderly to a suffering people: he will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry; when he hears it, he will answer you. Though the Lord may give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your Teacher will not hide himself any more (Isaiah 30:19–20).

And then a beautiful promise: your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, this is the way; walk in it (Isaiah 30:21). God guides us, not always by showing the whole road, but by a quiet word at each turning.

In the Gospel Jesus goes about all the cities and villages, teaching, proclaiming the good news and curing every sickness. When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. He tells his disciples: the harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few (Matthew 9:35–38).

Then he does something surprising: he calls the Twelve and sends them out to do what he has been doing. Proclaim the good news, cure the sick, cleanse lepers. You received without payment; give without payment (Matthew 10:8).

Advent is not only waiting for Christ; it is also being sent by him. The crowds of our time are harassed and helpless too: young people without direction, families under stress, people lost in addictions. Jesus looks at them with compassion, and he sends us.

Let us pray today for labourers in the harvest: priests, religious, catechists and committed lay people. Let us listen for that quiet word behind us: this is the way. And let us give freely what we have freely received. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus feels sorry for people who are lost and sad. Pray today that God will send many good priests and sisters!

homily: Dear friends, Isaiah paints a picture of joy: the wilderness and the dry land shall be glad, the desert shall rejoice and blossom. Strengthen the weak hands, make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who are of a fearful heart: be strong, do not fear! Here is your God (Isaiah 35:1–4).
He promises that the eyes of the blind will be opened, the lame will leap like a deer and the tongue of the speechless sing for joy (Isaiah 35:5–6). These are the signs of the Messiah.

In the Gospel some men bring a paralysed man on a bed to Jesus. The crowd is too great, so they go up on the roof and let him down through the tiles right in front of Jesus. When he saw their faith, he said: friend, your sins are forgiven you (Luke 5:18–20).

Notice: their faith. The paralysed man could not come by himself. His friends carried him, and they did not give up when the door was blocked. Jesus saw their faith and healed their friend. We can carry others to Jesus by our prayer and our love.
Notice too that Jesus first forgives sins, then heals the body. The deepest paralysis is sin. Then he says: stand up, take your bed and go home. And the man went home glorifying God (Luke 5:24–25).

Today we remember St Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who carried many to Christ, among them the young Augustine. Let us think of someone who cannot come to Jesus alone: a relative far from the faith, a sick friend, a struggling neighbour. Let us carry them in prayer this Advent, and not give up when the door seems blocked. Amen.
kids: Children, four friends carried a sick man to Jesus. You can carry your friends to Jesus by praying for them!

homily: Dear friends, Isaiah asks: to whom then will you compare me? Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He who brings out their host and numbers them, calling them all by name (Isaiah 40:25–26). The God of countless stars knows each one by name. He knows you by name too.

Then Isaiah answers the complaint of a tired people: why do you say, my way is hidden from the Lord? The Lord is the everlasting God. He does not faint or grow weary. He gives power to the faint. Those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint (Isaiah 40:27–31).

In the Gospel Jesus says one of his most loved invitations: come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:28–29).

Many of us are tired: parents juggling work and children, students under pressure, workers abroad, the sick, the old, the caregivers. December can make us even more tired with its rush. Jesus does not say: try harder. He says: come to me.
A yoke is a wooden frame that joins two oxen so that they pull together. Jesus offers to share our yoke. We do not carry life alone. His yoke is easy because he carries most of the weight.

This Advent, let us find a little time each day simply to rest in the Lord: a quiet moment in a church, a visit to the Blessed Sacrament, five minutes of silence. Those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength. Amen.
kids: Children, when you are tired or sad, Jesus says: come to me. You can always tell Him how you feel!

homily: Dear friends, God speaks through Isaiah with great tenderness: do not fear, you worm Jacob, you insect Israel! I will help you, says the Lord; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel (Isaiah 41:14). God calls his people a worm, not to insult them but to show how small and weak they feel, and how strong he is for them.
He promises: I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys; I will make the wilderness a pool of water (Isaiah 41:18). God turns dryness into life.
In the Gospel Jesus praises John the Baptist: among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist. Yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he (Matthew 11:11).

How can the least be greater than John? Not because we are holier than John, but because we live after the coming of Christ. We have received what John only announced: the death and resurrection of Jesus, baptism, the Holy Spirit, the Eucharist. We are given more than the greatest prophet.

This should give us both gratitude and responsibility. If we have received so much, how much more should we bear fruit? John lived in the desert on locusts and wild honey and gave his life for the truth. What do we give?

When you feel small, remember: God says, do not fear, I will help you. And when you feel proud, remember: all you have is gift. Let us thank God today for the riches of the Kingdom, and use them generously this Advent. Amen.
kids: Children, God holds your hand like a loving father. You never walk alone!

homily: Dear friends, God speaks through Isaiah like a sad father: I am the Lord your God, who teaches you for your own good, who leads you in the way you should go. O that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your prosperity would have been like a river, and your success like the waves of the sea (Isaiah 48:17–18).
God's commandments are not burdens to restrict us; they are a teacher's guidance for our own good. When we ignore them, we lose the river of peace he wanted to give us.

In the Gospel Jesus compares his generation to children in the marketplace: we played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we wailed, and you did not mourn. John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, he has a demon. The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, look, a glutton and a drunkard (Matthew 11:16–19).
Whatever God does, some people find an excuse not to respond. John was too strict; Jesus was too friendly. The real problem was not John or Jesus; it was hearts that did not want to change.

We too can be like those children. The homily is too long; the priest is too strict; the Church is not modern enough; I will pray when life is easier. Behind our complaints, there is often a heart that does not want to be disturbed.

Jesus ends: wisdom is vindicated by her deeds (Matthew 11:19). The proof of faith is its fruit. This Advent, let us stop making excuses and let God's word lead us in the way we should go. Then our peace will be like a river. Amen.
kids: Children, God's commandments are like a loving teacher who wants you to be happy. Obey them with joy!

homily: Dear friends, Sirach remembers the prophet Elijah: then Elijah arose, a prophet like fire, and his word burned like a torch (Sirach 48:1). He was taken up in a whirlwind of fire, and the tradition said he would return to turn the hearts of parents to their children (Sirach 48:9–10).

In the Gospel, as they come down from the mountain of the Transfiguration, the disciples ask Jesus about Elijah. Jesus answers: Elijah has already come, and they did not recognise him, but did to him whatever they pleased. Then the disciples understood that he was speaking about John the Baptist (Matthew 17:10–13).
John came in the spirit and power of Elijah. Both were men of fire: they spoke the truth whatever the cost. Both called the people back to God. Both suffered for it.

Today is also the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe. In 1531 Mary appeared to a poor indigenous man, St Juan Diego, near Mexico City, as a young mother, dressed like his own people, expecting a child (T). Through her, millions came to faith. She is patroness of the Americas and of the unborn.
Elijah and John prepared the way by fiery words; Mary at Guadalupe prepared the way with a mother's tenderness. God uses both fire and gentleness to turn hearts.

Elijah was to turn the hearts of parents to their children. This is a great need today: parents too busy for their children, children too distant from their parents. This Advent, let us turn our hearts to our families: time, attention, forgiveness. And let us ask Our Lady of Guadalupe to protect all mothers and their unborn children. Amen.
kids: Children, Mary appeared to a poor man named Juan Diego and spoke his language. Mary loves every people and every child!

homily: Dear friends, in the first reading a pagan prophet, Balaam, is hired by a king to curse Israel. Instead, the Spirit of God comes upon him and he blesses them. He sees from afar: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17). God can speak even through unexpected people.

The Church has always seen in this star a prophecy of Christ, and of the star that led the Magi to Bethlehem. Balaam saw him, but not now; beheld him, but not near. We, who have seen him come near, are more blessed.

In the Gospel the chief priests and elders challenge Jesus: by what authority are you doing these things? Jesus answers with a question: did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin? They reason: if we say from heaven, he will ask why we did not believe; if we say of human origin, we fear the crowd. So they answer: we do not know (Matthew 21:23–27).
They were not really seeking the truth; they were calculating. Their answer depended on what was safe, not on what was true. Jesus would not play their game.

Today we remember St John of the Cross, who was imprisoned by his own brothers for seeking reform, yet in his dark cell wrote some of the most beautiful poems of love for God. He did not calculate; he gave everything.

Do I sometimes calculate in matters of faith? I will speak about God only if it is safe; I will go to Mass if there is nothing better to do; I will forgive if they apologise first. This Advent let us seek the truth honestly and follow it, like the star of Jacob, wherever it leads. Amen.
kids: Children, a star led the wise men to Jesus. Ask Jesus to be the bright star that guides you every day!

homily: Dear friends, the prophet Zephaniah speaks of a city that is rebellious and defiled: it has listened to no voice, it has accepted no correction (Zephaniah 3:1–2). Then God promises: I will leave in the midst of you a people humble and lowly. They shall seek refuge in the name of the Lord (Zephaniah 3:12).
God's future belongs to the humble: the anawim, the poor of the Lord. Mary, Joseph, the shepherds, Simeon and Anna belong to this humble remnant who waited for the Messiah.

In the Gospel Jesus tells a parable. A man has two sons. He asks the first to work in the vineyard; he says, I will not, but later changes his mind and goes. He asks the second; he says, I go, sir, but does not go. Which of the two did the will of his father? (Matthew 21:28–31).

Then Jesus says something shocking to the religious leaders: the tax collectors and prostitutes are going into the kingdom of God ahead of you. For John came in the way of righteousness, and they believed him, but you did not (Matthew 21:31–32).

The second son represents those who say yes with their lips but no with their lives. The first son represents sinners who first say no but then repent. Both are in us. We say yes at Mass, then no at home. We refuse God, and then, by grace, we change our minds.

It is never too late to change our minds. This Advent, let us be the son who repents. Let us look honestly at where we have said yes but not gone, and go now. And let us ask to belong to the humble remnant who seek refuge in the Lord. Amen.
kids: Children, one son said no but then obeyed; the other said yes but did not. Jesus wants us to say yes and then really do it!

homily: Dear friends, Isaiah proclaims: I am the Lord, and there is no other. Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the skies rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation may spring up (Isaiah 45:6, 8). The Church has sung this verse for centuries in Advent as the Rorate caeli: heaven drops down its dew, and the earth gives birth to the Saviour.
God says: turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear (Isaiah 45:22–23). The Saviour is for all nations.

In the Gospel John the Baptist, in prison, sends his disciples to ask Jesus: are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another? Even John had questions. Jesus answers: go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news brought to them. And blessed is anyone who takes no offence at me (Luke 7:20–23).
Jesus does not give John a theory; he points to signs. Isaiah had foretold them. Where the Messiah is, people are healed and the poor hear good news.

Today too, people ask the Church: are you the one? Is Christ real? The best answer is not argument, but signs: hospitals, schools, care for the poor, families transformed, sinners forgiven, lives given in love. Our deeds must show that the Messiah has come.

Blessed is anyone who takes no offence at me. Some were offended because Jesus was not the Messiah they expected. This Advent, let us accept Jesus as he is, not as we want him to be, and let our lives become signs that he has come. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus showed who He was by healing and helping people. We show we love Jesus by helping others too!

homily: Dear friends, from today the Church enters the last week before Christmas. At Evening Prayer she begins to sing the great O Antiphons. Tonight's is: O Wisdom, coming forth from the mouth of the Most High, reaching from end to end and ordering all things mightily and sweetly: come and teach us the way of prudence.

In the first reading the dying Jacob blesses his sons and says of Judah: the sceptre shall not depart from Judah, until tribute comes to him; and the obedience of the peoples is his (Genesis 49:10). From the tribe of Judah would come David, and from David the Messiah.

The Gospel gives us the genealogy of Jesus: Abraham was the father of Isaac, Isaac the father of Jacob, and so on through forty-two generations to Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah (Matthew 1:1–16).

We may be tempted to skip this long list of names. But it is full of meaning. It includes great saints like Abraham and David, and great sinners too. It includes four women, some of them foreigners, and one whose story involved adultery. God's plan passed through all of them.

This tells us that God can write salvation through crooked lines. Our family history may have its own sins, wounds and shames. God is not ashamed to enter it. Jesus took a real human family tree, with all its brokenness, to heal it from within.

Today, let us thank God for our ancestors who handed on the faith, and pray for those in our family line who need healing and mercy. And let us pray with the Church: O Wisdom, come and teach us the way of prudence. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus had grandparents and great-grandparents, just like you. Pray today for your whole family!

homily: Dear friends, today's O Antiphon prays: O Adonai, ruler of the house of Israel, who appeared to Moses in the flame of the burning bush and gave him the law on Sinai: come and redeem us with outstretched arm.

Jeremiah announces: the days are surely coming, says the Lord, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and shall execute justice and righteousness in the land. And this is the name by which he will be called: The Lord is our righteousness (Jeremiah 23:5–6).

In the Gospel we meet St Joseph. Mary is found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly. But an angel says to him in a dream: Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife (Matthew 1:18–20).

Joseph's righteousness is not cold legalism. Even before the angel speaks, his justice is merciful: he will not shame Mary. Then, when God speaks, he obeys immediately: when Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel commanded him (Matthew 1:24).

The angel tells him to name the child Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins, and calls him Emmanuel, God is with us (Matthew 1:21–23). Joseph gives Jesus his name and his place in the house of David. Without words, he serves God's plan.

Joseph is a model for fathers and for all of us: just and merciful, attentive to God's voice, quick to obey, faithful in silence. This Christmas, let us ask St Joseph to help us make room for Jesus in our homes, and not to be afraid. Amen.
kids: Children, Joseph listened to the angel and took care of Mary and baby Jesus. Ask St Joseph to help you obey God!

homily: Dear friends, today's O Antiphon prays: O Root of Jesse, standing as a sign for the peoples, before whom kings shall keep silent: come to deliver us and delay no longer.

In the first reading the wife of Manoah is barren. An angel appears and tells her she will bear a son, Samson, who will be a Nazirite, consecrated to God from birth, and he will begin to save Israel (Judges 13:2–5). God brings life where there was none.

In the Gospel the angel Gabriel appears to the old priest Zechariah in the Temple: your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will name him John. He will turn many of the people of Israel to the Lord their God (Luke 1:13–16).
But Zechariah doubts: how will I know that this is so? For I am an old man, and my wife is getting on in years (Luke 1:18). Because he did not believe, he becomes mute until the child is born.

Zechariah had prayed for years. When the answer finally came, he could not believe it. How often we pray without really expecting God to answer! Elizabeth, on the other hand, says: this is what the Lord has done for me; he has taken away my disgrace (Luke 1:25).

As Christmas draws near, let us renew our faith in prayer. God hears. His timing is not ours, but he hears. Let us keep praying for what we long for, and when God answers, in his way, let us believe and give thanks. Amen.
kids: Children, Zechariah prayed for a long time, and God answered. Keep praying, even if the answer takes time!

homily: Dear friends, today's O Antiphon prays: O Dayspring, splendour of eternal light and sun of justice: come and enlighten those who dwell in darkness and the shadow of death.

The Song of Songs sings of love: the voice of my beloved! Look, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away; for now the winter is past (Song of Songs 2:8, 10–11). The Church reads it in Advent as God coming to his people with the eagerness of love.

In the Gospel Mary sets out and goes with haste to the hill country, to the house of Zechariah, and greets Elizabeth. When Elizabeth hears Mary's greeting, the child leaps in her womb, and Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit. She exclaims: blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And blessed is she who believed (Luke 1:39–45).

Mary carries Jesus hidden within her, and wherever she goes, joy follows. John the Baptist leaps for joy even before birth. Elizabeth is filled with the Spirit. The Visitation is the first Christmas in a way: Christ arrives at a home, and the home is transformed.
We too carry Christ, especially after Holy Communion. When we visit others with love, Christ comes with us. A visit to a sick neighbour, a lonely grandparent, a family in grief, can be a Visitation.

Elizabeth praises Mary above all for her faith: blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfilment of what was spoken to her by the Lord (Luke 1:45). This Christmas, let us believe God's promises, and carry Christ with haste to someone who needs his joy. Amen.
kids: Children, Mary visited her cousin and brought Jesus with her. When you visit someone with love, you bring Jesus too!

homily: Dear friends, today's O Antiphon prays: O King of the nations, and their desire, the cornerstone who makes both one: come and save the human race, which you fashioned from clay.

In the first reading Hannah brings the young Samuel to the house of the Lord at Shiloh. She had prayed for a child; now she gives him back: for this child I prayed, and the Lord has granted me the petition that I made to him. Therefore I have lent him to the Lord (1 Samuel 1:27–28). Then Hannah sings: my heart exults in the Lord (1 Samuel 2:1).

In the Gospel Mary sings her Magnificat: my soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour, for he has looked with favour on the lowliness of his servant (Luke 1:46–48). Hannah's song and Mary's song are sisters: both praise the God who lifts up the lowly.

Mary sings that God has brought down the powerful from their thrones and lifted up the lowly; he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty (Luke 1:52–53). This is God's way: he chooses the small.
Hannah gave back the gift she had received. Mary gave her whole self. Both teach us that what God gives us is not ours to keep, but to offer back to him: our children, our talents, our lives.

Let us pray the Magnificat slowly today, perhaps as a family. Let us give back to God one gift he has given us, by using it for others. And let us ask Mary to give us humble, grateful hearts as we approach Christmas. Amen.
kids: Children, Mary sang a song of joy because God loves the poor and the humble. Sing a song to God today!

homily: Dear friends, today's O Antiphon, the last, prays: O Emmanuel, our King and Lawgiver, the hope of the nations and their Saviour: come and save us, O Lord our God. Read backwards, the first letters of the antiphons in Latin spell ERO CRAS: tomorrow I will be there (T).

Malachi announces: see, I am sending my messenger to prepare the way before me, and the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. Then he promises to send the prophet Elijah, who will turn the hearts of parents to their children and the hearts of children to their parents (Malachi 3:1, 23–24).

In the Gospel Elizabeth gives birth to her son. Neighbours and relatives want to name him Zechariah after his father. But Elizabeth says: no; he is to be called John. They ask Zechariah, and he writes on a tablet: his name is John. Immediately his mouth is opened and he begins to speak, praising God (Luke 1:57–64).

John means God is gracious. The name was not chosen by family custom but by God. Zechariah's obedience, writing the name God gave, loosened his tongue. When we obey God, even after doubting, our lips are opened for praise.
The people asked: what then will this child become? For the hand of the Lord was with him (Luke 1:66). Every child is a mystery and a promise. Every child is born with God's hand upon them.

On the eve of Christmas Eve, let us obey God in whatever he has asked and we have delayed. Let us turn our hearts to our families, as Malachi says. And let us pray with longing: O Emmanuel, come. Tomorrow I will be there. Amen.
kids: Children, Zechariah could not speak until he obeyed God; then he praised God. When we obey God, our hearts are happy!

homily: Dear friends, this morning Mass on Christmas Eve is the last Mass of Advent. The first reading recalls God's promise to David: when your days are fulfilled, I will raise up your offspring after you, and I will establish his kingdom. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me. Your throne shall be established for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16).

In the Gospel Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, sings the Benedictus: blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has looked favourably on his people and redeemed them. He has raised up a mighty saviour for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:68–69).
The Church sings this song every morning at Lauds. Today it has special meaning. The promise to David is about to be fulfilled tonight in Bethlehem, the city of David.

Zechariah sings that we are saved so that we might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days (Luke 1:74–75). Christmas is not only a feast to enjoy; it is a call to holiness, a life of serving God without fear.

He ends: by the tender mercy of our God, the dawn from on high will break upon us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace (Luke 1:78–79). Tonight the dawn breaks.

In the busyness of this day, cooking, cleaning, shopping, travelling, let us keep a moment of quiet. Let us pray the Benedictus, thank God for his faithfulness, and prepare our hearts for the Child who comes tonight. Amen.
kids: Children, tonight Jesus comes like the sunrise after a long night. Get your heart ready with a prayer!

intro: Theme: “Prepare the way of the Lord.”
God comforts; repentance prepares the road; John points to Christ who baptises with the Spirit.

sub: The exile is over.
God speaks tenderly.
His first word to sinners is comfort.
q: Comfort, O comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and cry to her that she has served her term, that her penalty is paid, that she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins.
Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
points.apply: Speak tenderly to someone who is discouraged.

sub: A highway in the desert.
Repentance levels pride and fills discouragement.
The crowds confessed their sins.
q: A voice cries out: “In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.”
John the baptizer appeared in the wilderness, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
points.apply: Make an Advent Confession.

points.h: He will baptize with the Holy Spirit
sub: John is unworthy to untie his sandals.
He points away from himself.
Christ gives the Spirit.
q: He will feed his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms, and carry them in his bosom, and gently lead the mother sheep.

He proclaimed, “The one who is more powerful than I is coming after me; I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the thong of his sandals. I have baptized you with water; but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”
points.apply: Do one good deed without seeking credit.

concl: God's patience is time for conversion.
Prepare the road; the King is coming.
2026-12-06.resolve: Begin the conversion you have postponed.

intro: Theme: “Rejoice: the Lord is near.”
Christ fulfils Isaiah's good news, gives the joy of the humble, and stands among us unrecognised.

sub: Isaiah's servant is anointed by the Spirit.
Jesus reads this at Nazareth.
Our joy has a name: Jesus.
q: The spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the oppressed, to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to the prisoners; to proclaim the year of the LORD's favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to let the oppressed go free, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.
points.apply: Visit someone sick or lonely before Christmas.

sub: Rose vestments, rose candle.
Mary's joy is the joy of the humble.
Thanksgiving in all circumstances.
q: Sing aloud, O daughter Zion; shout, O Israel! Rejoice and exult with all your heart, O daughter Jerusalem!
For the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name. His mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.
points.apply: Thank God for three joys every night.

points.h: One whom you do not know
sub: John is only a voice.
Christ is already among us.
We must learn to recognise him.
q: I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my whole being shall exult in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness.
John answered them, “I baptize with water. Among you stands one whom you do not know, the one who is coming after me; I am not worthy to untie the thong of his sandal.”
points.apply: Look for Christ in someone you overlook.

concl: Christian joy rests on God's faithfulness.
He who calls you is faithful.
2026-12-13.resolve: Pray a short prayer each time you pick up your phone this week.

intro: Theme: “Let it be with me.”
God builds David a house; the promise is fulfilled in Mary; Mary's yes opens the door to Christmas.

sub: David wants to build God a house.
God promises to build David a house.
God's gifts exceed our plans.
q: Your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me; your throne shall be established forever.

And now, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will name him Jesus. He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give to him the throne of his ancestor David. He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.
points.apply: Make room for God in one part of your day.

sub: Mary asks how.
The Spirit overshadows her.
The virgin conceives the Son of God.
q: Is anything too wonderful for the LORD? At the set time I will return to you, in due season, and Sarah shall have a son.

Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, since I am a virgin?” The angel said to her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be holy; he will be called Son of God.”
points.apply: Bring an “impossible” situation to God in prayer.

sub: Samuel listened.
Mary consented freely.
Our Amen at Communion echoes hers.
q: Now the LORD came and stood there, calling as before, “Samuel! Samuel!” And Samuel said, “Speak, for your servant is listening.”
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.” Then the angel departed from her.
points.apply: Pray the Angelus three times a day.

concl: God wants to make his home in us.
With Mary, let us say yes.
2026-12-20.resolve: Set up the crib as a family before Christmas Eve.

intro: Theme: “The Word became flesh.”
God's final word is a Child; the eternal Son became man to make us children of God.

sub: In the beginning was the Word.
He became flesh and lived among us.
True God and true man.
q: For a child has been born for us, a son given to us; authority rests upon his shoulders; and he is named Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father's only son, full of grace and truth.
points.apply: Kneel at the crib with your family.

sub: Many words through the prophets.
One final Word in the Son.
The Word is love in the form of a child.
q: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news, who announces salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns.”

Long ago God spoke to our ancestors in many and various ways by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also created the worlds.
points.apply: Read the Christmas Gospel slowly today.

sub: His own did not receive him.
To those who received him he gave power.
No room in the inn: is there room in us?
q: But you, O Bethlehem of Ephrathah, who are one of the little clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to rule in Israel, whose origin is from of old, from ancient days.
He came to what was his own, and his own people did not accept him. But to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave power to become children of God.
points.apply: Invite someone lonely to your Christmas meal.

concl: God became what we are so that we might share what he is.
Christian, remember your dignity.
2026-12-25.resolve: Visit the crib in church during the Christmas octave.

intro: Theme: “The child grew and became strong.”
A family of faith, a child presented to the Lord, and the hidden holiness of Nazareth.

sub: Abraham and Sarah were old and childless.
God promised descendants like the stars.
Faith is the foundation of the home.
q: He brought him outside and said, “Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Then he said to him, “So shall your descendants be.” And he believed the LORD; and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.
By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to set out for a place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he set out, not knowing where he was going.
points.apply: Begin or renew daily family prayer.

sub: The firstborn belongs to God.
Mary and Joseph offer the gift of the poor.
Simeon foretells the sword.
q: Consecrate to me all the firstborn; whatever is the first to open the womb among the Israelites, of human beings and animals, is mine.

Then Simeon blessed them and said to his mother Mary, “This child is destined for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be opposed so that the inner thoughts of many will be revealed—and a sword will pierce your own soul too.”
points.apply: Offer your children to God in prayer today.

sub: Jesus obeyed Mary and Joseph.
He grew in wisdom and grace.
Faith is passed on at home.
q: Keep these words that I am commanding you today in your heart. Recite them to your children and talk about them when you are at home and when you are away, when you lie down and when you rise.

Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. His mother treasured all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in years, and in divine and human favor.
points.apply: Read a Gospel passage together at home this week.

concl: God chose a family; families find God at home.
Jesus, Mary and Joseph, make our homes like yours.
2026-12-27.resolve: Consecrate your family to the Holy Family this week.

intro: Theme: “A shoot from the stump.”
God starts again from what seems dead; his Spirit rests on the Messiah; the little ones see.

sub: David's family tree was cut down.
A shoot springs up.
God begins again where we see an end.
q: A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse, and a branch shall grow out of his roots. The spirit of the LORD shall rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.

At that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.”
points.apply: Bring one “dead stump” in your life to God in prayer.

sub: Wolf and lamb live together.
Enemies are reconciled.
Christ's peace begins in hearts.
q: The wolf shall live with the lamb, the leopard shall lie down with the kid, the calf and the lion and the fatling together.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.
points.apply: Make peace with one person this Advent.

points.h: Blessed are the eyes that see
sub: Prophets and kings longed to see.
We see Christ in Word and Sacrament.
Gratitude is the right response.
q: Many peoples shall come and say, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob; that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths.”

Then turning to the disciples, Jesus said to them privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, but did not see it, and to hear what you hear, but did not hear it.”
points.apply: Thank God tonight for the gift of faith.

concl: God's new beginnings come from small shoots.
Become little, and you will see.
2026-12-01.resolve: Pray “Come, Holy Spirit” each morning this Advent.

intro: Theme: “A feast for all peoples.”
God promises a feast; Jesus heals and feeds; the Eucharist sends us to the hungry.

sub: A banquet on the mountain.
Death swallowed up forever.
Tears wiped away.
q: On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wines, of rich food filled with marrow, of well-aged wines strained clear.

Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion for the crowd, because they have been with me now for three days and have nothing to eat; and I do not want to send them away hungry, for they might faint on the way.”
points.apply: Feed someone hungry this week.

sub: Jesus heals the lame, blind and mute.
God's promise is fulfilled in him.
Our sorrows are not the last word.
q: He will swallow up death forever. Then the Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from all faces, and the disgrace of his people he will take away from all the earth, for the LORD has spoken.
He will wipe every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; mourning and crying and pain will be no more, for the first things have passed away.
points.apply: Visit or call someone who is grieving.

sub: The words of the Last Supper.
Christ is the Bread from Bethlehem.
The disciples distribute.
q: The LORD is my shepherd, I shall not want.

He took the seven loaves and the fish; and after giving thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And all of them ate and were filled; and they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full.
points.apply: Say grace before every meal this Advent.

concl: Christ feeds us so that we may feed others.
The feast has begun at the altar.
2026-12-02.resolve: Prepare an Advent food basket for a poor family.

intro: Theme: “Built on rock.”
Not words but obedience; God the everlasting Rock; St Francis Xavier, a missionary built on Christ.

sub: Words alone are not faith.
The Father's will must be done.
Advent asks for concrete change.
q: Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And I said, “Here am I; send me!”
Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.
points.apply: Do one teaching of Jesus you have ignored.

sub: The same storms hit both houses.
The foundation decides.
God is the everlasting Rock.
q: Those of steadfast mind you keep in peace—in peace because they trust in you. Trust in the LORD forever, for in the LORD GOD you have an everlasting rock.

Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock. The rain fell, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on rock.
points.apply: Build a daily habit of reading the Gospel.

sub: He left Europe for India in 1542.
He preached on the coasts of South India.
He died in sight of China.
q: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news, who announces salvation.

Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything that I have commanded you. And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
points.apply: Support a missionary or mission diocese this Advent.

concl: Faith that acts is a house on rock.
Like Xavier, let Christ be our foundation.
2026-12-03.resolve: Give an Advent offering to the missions.

intro: Theme: “Do you believe?”
God promises sight; Jesus asks for faith; faith sees in the dark.

sub: Isaiah's great reversal.
The deaf hear, the blind see.
Advent is hope for transformation.
q: On that day the deaf shall hear the words of a scroll, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see.
Then he shouted, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”
points.apply: Pray for someone who cannot see God's hand in their life.

sub: The blind men followed and cried out.
Jesus asked a question.
Faith answered, “Yes, Lord.”
q: Those of steadfast mind you keep in peace—in peace because they trust in you.

When he entered the house, the blind men came to him; and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.” Then he touched their eyes and said, “According to your faith let it be done to you.”
points.apply: Say “Yes, Lord, I believe” about your deepest need.

sub: Faith sees in darkness.
The invisible God became visible in Christ.
We look on his face in prayer.
q: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father's only son, full of grace and truth.
points.apply: Spend time before the Blessed Sacrament today.

concl: Faith opens the eyes.
Christ is our light this Advent.
2026-12-04.resolve: Make a holy hour this First Friday or next week.

intro: Theme: “This is the way; walk in it.”
God waits to be gracious; Jesus has compassion; the Twelve are sent.

sub: He hears the cry of his people.
He shows the way.
He binds up wounds.
q: Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you; therefore he will rise up to show mercy to you. For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him.
When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.
points.apply: Bring your deepest cry to God today.

sub: Your Teacher will not hide.
A voice behind you guides.
Advent is about finding the way.
q: And when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left, your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, “This is the way; walk in it.”
The voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.’
points.apply: Ask God for guidance in one decision.

sub: The harvest is plentiful.
Pray for labourers.
Become a labourer yourself.
q: He heals the brokenhearted, and binds up their wounds.
Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. You received without payment; give without payment.
points.apply: Offer a free service to someone this week.

concl: God's compassion sends us out.
Walk in his way, and share what you have received.
2026-12-05.resolve: Pray each day of Advent for vocations from your parish.

intro: Theme: “Here is your God.”
God makes the desert bloom, friends carry the paralysed man, Christ forgives.

sub: Dry land rejoices.
Weak hands are strengthened.
God comes to save.
q: Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who are of a fearful heart, “Be strong, do not fear! Here is your God. He will come with vengeance, with terrible recompense. He will come and save you.”
Amazement seized all of them, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, “We have seen strange things today.”
points.apply: Encourage someone who is afraid.

sub: The friends would not give up.
They opened the roof.
Jesus saw their faith.
q: Then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the speechless sing for joy. For waters shall break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
When he saw their faith, he said, “Friend, your sins are forgiven you.”
points.apply: Pray daily for a friend in need.

sub: Forgiveness first, then healing.
Only God can forgive sins.
Christ gives this authority to his Church.
q: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits—who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the Pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy.
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—he said to the one who was paralyzed—“I say to you, stand up and take your bed and go to your home.”
points.apply: Go to Confession this Advent.

concl: God's coming makes everything bloom.
Let him forgive and raise you up.
2026-12-07.resolve: Bring someone with you to the parish Advent Confession service.

intro: Theme: “Full of grace.”
God promised the woman in Eden, preserved Mary from sin, and freed her to say yes.

points.h: Where are you? The first promise
sub: After the fall God seeks Adam.
He promises the woman and her offspring.
The serpent's head will be crushed.
q: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.
A great portent appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.
points.apply: Answer God's “Where are you?” in Confession.

sub: Mary is preserved, not rescued.
She is redeemed by Christ in a more exalted way.
God prepared a worthy home for his Son.
q: You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.
And he came to her and said, “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you.”
points.apply: Pray the Hail Mary slowly today.

sub: Grace frees Mary's freedom.
Eve's knot is untied by Mary's yes.
Our yes prepares for Christmas.
q: I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my whole being shall exult in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness.
For nothing will be impossible with God. Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.” Then the angel departed from her.
points.apply: Say yes to one thing God asks of you.

concl: God prepared Mary; he wants to prepare us.
With Mary, let us say yes.
2026-12-08.resolve: Pray the Rosary as a family this week.

intro: Theme: “Come to me.”
God never grows weary; Jesus gives rest; waiting on the Lord renews strength.

sub: The exiles felt forgotten.
The Creator names every star.
He gives power to the faint.
q: Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable. He gives power to the faint, and strengthens the powerless.
Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
points.apply: Tell God honestly where you are tired.

sub: A yoke shares the load.
Jesus is gentle and humble.
His burden is light because he carries it with us.
q: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits—who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
points.apply: Help carry someone else's load this week.

sub: Waiting on God is active trust.
God chose the humble Juan Diego.
He reveals himself to the little ones.
q: But those who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength, they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint.

At that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants.”
points.apply: Spend ten minutes in silent prayer today.

concl: The weary find rest in Christ.
Wait on the Lord, and rise.
2026-12-09.resolve: Visit the Blessed Sacrament once this week.

intro: Theme: “Do not fear, I will help you.”
God holds our hand, opens rivers in the desert, and makes the least great in his Kingdom.

sub: Israel felt like a worm.
God takes its hand.
Fear gives way to trust.
q: For I, the LORD your God, hold your right hand; it is I who say to you, “Do not fear, I will help you.”
And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
points.apply: Pray “Lord, hold me” when afraid today.

sub: The poor seek water.
God opens rivers on bare heights.
All will know his hand did it.
q: When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the LORD will answer them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys; I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water.
Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink. As the scripture has said, “Out of the believer's heart shall flow rivers of living water.”
points.apply: Bring a dry area of your life to Jesus.

sub: John is the greatest of the prophets.
He prepared the way.
Baptism makes us children of the Kingdom.
q: See, I am sending my messenger to prepare the way before me, and the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.
Truly I tell you, among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist; yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
points.apply: Thank God for your Baptism.

concl: God holds us by the hand.
Little ones are great in his Kingdom.
2026-12-10.resolve: Renew your baptismal promises before Christmas.

intro: Theme: “O that you had paid attention!”
God teaches for our good; excuses refuse every messenger; wisdom shows in deeds.

sub: God speaks like a longing father.
Obedience brings peace like a river.
The commandments are a gift.
q: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: I am the LORD your God, who teaches you for your own good, who leads you in the way you should go. O that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your prosperity would have been like a river, and your success like the waves of the sea.
The voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.’
points.apply: Read one commandment with the Catechism today.

sub: They would play neither wedding nor funeral.
John was too strict; Jesus too friendly.
Excuses can refuse every call.
q: Happy are those who do not follow the advice of the wicked, or take the path that sinners tread, or sit in the seat of scoffers; but their delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law they meditate day and night.

But to what will I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we wailed, and you did not mourn.’
points.apply: Drop one excuse you use with God.

sub: Jesus is a friend of sinners.
His deeds show his wisdom.
Our lives should show it too.
q: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord GOD, and not rather that they should turn from their ways and live?
The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.
points.apply: Befriend someone others avoid.

concl: Stop excusing; start responding.
Let God's wisdom show in your deeds.
2026-12-11.resolve: Make an Advent examination on the Ten Commandments.

intro: Theme: “Elijah has already come.”
Elijah's fire, John's unrecognised coming, and Mary who carries Christ to a people.

sub: Elijah's word burned.
He was taken up in a whirlwind.
He would return to prepare the way.
q: Then Elijah arose, a prophet like fire, and his word burned like a torch.

With the spirit and power of Elijah he will go before him, to turn the hearts of parents to their children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.
points.apply: Ask the Holy Spirit to set your words on fire for good.

sub: Elijah came in John.
Many missed him.
The Son of Man too will suffer.
q: Lo, I will send you the prophet Elijah before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes. He will turn the hearts of parents to their children and the hearts of children to their parents, so that I will not come and strike the land with a curse.

He replied, “Elijah is indeed coming and will restore all things; but I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but they did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man is about to suffer at their hands.”
points.apply: Reconcile with a family member before Christmas.

sub: She came to the humble Juan Diego.
Her image shows her with child.
She carries Christ to a whole people.
q: When they met her, they all blessed her with one accord and said to her, “You are the glory of Jerusalem, you are the great boast of Israel, you are the great pride of our nation!”
A great portent appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.
points.apply: Pray the Rosary for unborn children.

concl: God sends messengers to turn our hearts.
Mary brings Christ to us this Advent.
2026-12-12.resolve: Pray for the protection of unborn children this Advent.

intro: Theme: “A star shall come out of Jacob.”
God's promise shines from afar; Christ's authority is from heaven; truth asks for honesty.

sub: Balaam came to curse and blessed.
He saw the star from afar.
The Magi followed that star.
q: I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near—a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall crush the borderlands of Moab, and the territory of all the Shethites.
Asking, “Where is the child who has been born king of the Jews? For we observed his star at its rising, and have come to pay him homage.”
points.apply: Put up your Christmas star with a prayer.

sub: The leaders challenged Jesus.
His authority is from the Father.
He teaches as no one else.
q: Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths. Lead me in your truth, and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation; for you I wait all day long.
When he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came to him as he was teaching, and said, “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?”
points.apply: Let Christ's word have authority in one decision.

sub: The leaders calculated.
They refused to answer.
Truth requires honesty.
q: See, I am sending my messenger to prepare the way before me, and the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.
Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin? And they argued with one another, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’”
points.apply: Face one truth you have avoided.

concl: The star is rising; answer honestly.
In the evening of life we will be judged on love.
2026-12-14.resolve: Make a quiet holy hour this week.

intro: Theme: “Words or deeds?”
